extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students/scholars of comedy and popular culture
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative criteria and stylistic features of stand-up comedy and comic legacy from a biographical article on Robin Williams. Focuses on what made his performances influential and how peers and critics judged his work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Onstage energy and improvisational skill
rubrics_metrics.description: “Williams's onstage energy and improvisational skill became a model for a new generation of stand-up comedians.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators value high physical and vocal energy onstage and strong improvisational ability; these are treated as hallmark indicators of an influential stand-up performer. Examples in the text: his rapid character changes and spontaneous reactions that inspired younger comedians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working highly personal issues into material (honesty)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Many comedians valued the way he worked highly personal issues into his comedy routines, especially his honesty about drug and alcohol addiction, along with depression.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using frank, personal subject matter (addiction, mental health, etc.) is presented as a quality that deepens material and influences peers. This is a positive criterion: personal honesty can create resonance and authenticity in comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature free-form comedy persona
rubrics_metrics.description: “Williams created a signature free-form comedy persona so widely and uniquely identified that new comedians like Jim Carrey impersonated him, paving the way for the growing comedy scene...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A distinctive, free-form persona that blends characters and modes is seen as a strength; it can become a model for others and help expand a local comedy scene. Originality of persona is prized; the page cites imitation (impersonation) as evidence of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quick‑fire / 'synaptic' delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted: “Usually, you start off performing in bars... So I developed a style that was very much synaptic: quick-firing, moving, so that they never really had a chance to lock on as a target.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid pace, quick transitions, and breathless delivery are identified as stylistic markers that keep audiences off-balance and engaged. This criterion favors performers who maintain momentum and surprise through speed and agility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of free association and improvisation to sustain interest
rubrics_metrics.description: “He often used free association of ideas while improvising to keep the audience interested.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques such as associative leaps and in-the-moment improvisation are judged positively for maintaining engagement. Evaluators should note how performers connect disparate ideas fluidly and respond spontaneously to the room.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity and manic style (risk/edge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Biographer's description: “intense, utterly manic style of stand-up [which sometimes] defies analysis ... [going] beyond energetic, beyond frenetic ... [and sometimes] dangerous ... because of what it said about the creator's own mental state.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An extremely intense or manic performance style can be a double-edged quality: it may be seen as extraordinary and compelling, but also as risky or indicative of personal instability. Critics may flag 'too intense' as a potential flaw or danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and avoidance of joke theft
rubrics_metrics.description: Context: accusations that Williams 'stolen their jokes' prompted him to avoid other comedians' shows; Whoopi Goldberg noted reuse 'is done all the time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original material is an ethical and reputational criterion. Even where reuse is common, being perceived as derivative or as taking others' jokes harms standing among peers. Evaluators should weigh originality of content and respect for other comedians' material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility and breadth across dramatic and comedic roles
rubrics_metrics.description: “Although Williams was first recognized as a stand-up comedian and television star, he became known for acting in film roles of substance and serious drama.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ability to perform convincingly in both comedy and drama is a marker of acting excellence and legacy. Assessors should note range of roles, depth of dramatic work, and impact on peers and audiences beyond stand-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence as an uncopyable standard (raising the bar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judd Apatow: “You can't look at any modern comic and say, 'That's the descendant of Robin Williams'... He raised the bar for what it's possible to do...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An artist's influence can be measured not just by imitation but by having expanded expectations for the field. This criterion values contributions that change what peers consider possible even if they cannot be directly replicated.
